briefing.text: First check whether the hypothesis is about this study: confirm that the cohort is gallbladder carcinoma (CANCER_TYPE / CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED), that SMAD4 and STK11 appear in the genomic tables, and which survival columns exist. Under the task's labelling convention, a hypothesis about this study's cancer type and genes is labelled True or False, not Not verifiable, even when a needed variable is missing. The claim is joint: it says BOTH genes are independently associated with reduced survival, so judge each gene on its own and then judge the claim as a whole.
briefing.reason: Calling it 'Not verifiable' by mistake is the commonest way to get the label wrong, and the claim covers two genes, which changes how a result for one gene should be weighed.

briefing.text: 'Independently associated' requires a multivariable Cox model of overall survival that includes SMAD4 status, STK11 status and clinical covariates (stage, age, sex where available); a univariable log-rank test does not establish independence. Check events per variable (about 10 or more) and the proportional-hazards assumption (Schoenfeld residuals). If STK11 is altered in very few patients, its estimate will be unstable: use Firth-penalised Cox or report it as underpowered, give HRs with 95% CIs, and do not read a wide CI as proof of no effect.
briefing.reason: This sets which test the word 'independently' actually calls for, and how to handle a gene that is rarely altered.

briefing.text: The hypothesis concerns METASTATIC gallbladder carcinoma, but the cohort probably mixes localised/resected and metastatic disease, and stage confounds both alteration frequency and survival. Identify metastatic patients (stage IV at diagnosis or collection, SAMPLE_TYPE=Metastasis, metastatic-site fields). Run the primary analysis in the metastatic subset and a stage-adjusted analysis in the full cohort, and report both.
briefing.reason: Analysing the wrong population, or skipping the stage adjustment, can create or hide the association being tested.

briefing.text: In MSK-IMPACT cohorts tumours are often sequenced months or years after diagnosis. Overall survival measured from diagnosis without accounting for this gives left-truncation (immortal-time) bias that favours genotypes sequenced late. Look at the diagnosis-to-sample-collection interval (for example OS_MONTHS_DIAG_TO_COLL) next to the OS time variable. If gaps are common, fit Cox with delayed entry (start = time from diagnosis to collection, stop = OS time) or measure OS from sequencing, and report whether the SMAD4/STK11 hazard ratios change.
briefing.reason: This bias can move the hazard ratios in either direction, so it bears directly on the survival result.

briefing.text: Define gene alteration from all sources. SMAD4 is often inactivated by homozygous deletion (data_cna.txt = -2), and STK11 by deletion or truncation. Combine non-synonymous mutations (exclude Silent/Intron/UTR) with deep deletions (and disruptive SVs from data_sv.txt) for each gene, and tabulate counts by source. Use 'oncogenic mutation OR deep deletion' as the main definition and run a mutation-only sensitivity analysis.
briefing.reason: Counting mutations alone undercounts carriers and moves patients into the wrong group, especially for SMAD4.

briefing.text: Samples may have been sequenced on different MSK-IMPACT panels. Use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt to confirm that SMAD4 and STK11 were profiled on every panel used. Exclude a sample whose panel lacks a gene rather than coding it wild-type for that gene.
briefing.reason: Treating an unprofiled sample as wild-type puts patients in the wrong comparison group.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume the survival time and survival status columns they used belong together (same origin, same follow-up date); the patient table holds OS_STATUS/OS_MONTHS (100 with status), CRDB_SURVIVAL_STATUS (92 with status, different consent/follow-up basis), and the sample table holds OVERALL_SURVIVAL_MONTHS (collection to follow-up) and OS_MONTHS_DIAGNOSIS_TO_FU for ~230 samples. Team B combined two status columns with an OS-from-diagnosis time without showing they share an end date.

Both assume 'metastatic gallbladder carcinoma' equals one of: stage IV at collection, a metastasis-site sample, or patients having OS data; the significant results depend on which definition is used and neither justified the choice from the task wording.

Both treat all histologies as one population (208 adenocarcinoma, 22 adenosquamous, plus neuroendocrine/small-cell/squamous/mixed); neuroendocrine carcinomas have different biology and prognosis and could confound gene-survival associations.
Both assume a CNA deep deletion (-2) is equivalent to a nonsynonymous mutation as a 'variant'; Team A's SMAD4 signal largely depends on including deletions.
unused_evidence: CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED (histology subtype, incl. neuroendocrine) - not used as covariate or exclusion by either team.
TUMOR_STAGE_COLLECTION / SAMPLE_TYPE / METASTATIC_SITE - used to define subgroups but not as adjustment covariates for 'independence' in the full cohort (Team B).
OS_MONTHS_DIAG_TO_COLL - Team A used it for delayed entry; Team B did not, although OS from diagnosis with sequencing later creates left truncation.

Other drivers and tumour features (TP53, KRAS, ERBB2, CDKN2A, TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS, MSI, TUMOR_PURITY) - 'independently' could mean independent of other prognostic genomic features, but neither team adjusted for them; low purity could also hide deletions/mutations.
data_cna_hg19.seg and SV table - Team B did not use SVs; neither checked SMAD4 heterozygous loss or segment-level calls.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: STK11 rests on ~10 altered patients and loses significance under delayed entry (p=0.17) and mutation-only definition - reported, not resolved.
Team B: significance appears only in the metastatic-sample subgroup; stage IV and all-patient analyses are not significant; ~1/3 of patients lack status - reported, not resolved.
Neither team showed the STK11 result is not driven by a few short-survival outliers or by the coupling of STK11 with other alterations (e.g. KRAS).
second_readings: 'Independently' may mean each gene is prognostic independent of the other and of clinical covariates (stage, histology, age), not merely both entered in one model with age.
'Metastatic gallbladder carcinoma' may mean the stage IV / metastatic-disease cohort (the clinical setting), not samples taken from a metastatic site.
'Variants' may mean somatic mutations only, which changes the SMAD4 result in Team A's sensitivity analysis.
'Reduced survival' could be overall survival from diagnosis or from sequencing (collection); the two time scales give different risk sets.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust: both teams find HR>1 for both genes, but significance depends on the subgroup, the alteration definition and how survival is handled. Neither has checked that their survival columns belong together or adjusted for histology and other drivers. The agreement may come from the same fragile choices rather than from robust evidence.

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED by SMAD4 and STK11 status in your stage IV cohort and rerun the multivariable Cox restricted to adenocarcinoma (or adjusted for histology): does the STK11 or SMAD4 effect persist, and does this change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Add other common drivers (e.g. TP53, KRAS, ERBB2, CDKN2A) and TMB/purity as covariates, and check co-occurrence of STK11 with KRAS: does 'independent' association of either gene survive, and does the result change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: For the ~10 STK11-altered patients, list survival time, event, stage, histology and alteration type; does a leave-one-out Cox show the STK11 HR is driven by one or two patients, and does that change how you weigh the data versus the study's reported finding?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You combined two survival-status columns (OS_STATUS and CRDB_SURVIVAL_STATUS) with an OS-from-diagnosis time. For patients with both, do they agree, and do they refer to the same follow-up date as the time you used? Does using one internally consistent time/status pair change your results or method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your OS is measured from diagnosis but sequencing happened later (OS_MONTHS_DIAG_TO_COLL). Does a delayed-entry (left-truncated) Cox, or OS from collection, change the SMAD4/STK11 hazard ratios in your metastatic subgroup, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: In the full cohort, does a Cox model with both genes adjusted for stage at collection, sample type and histology (CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED) give the same direction and strength as your subgroup analyses, and does that change which cohort definition you rely on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You did not use data_sv.txt. Does adding SMAD4/STK11 structural variants, or using mutations only, reclassify any patient and change the hazard ratios in your primary subgroup? Does that change your method?

findings.question: In cBioPortal-style clinical tables from institutional clinical sequencing cohorts, how are OS_MONTHS measured (from diagnosis or from sequencing/collection), and is the status column defined at the same follow-up date as the months column?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (4 attempted), so no page was read. Background knowledge only: in MSK clinical-sequencing studies, patient-level OS_MONTHS is usually counted from diagnosis (some studies count from sequencing, so read the '#' description lines), and OS_STATUS is recorded at the same last follow-up as its paired months column. Other columns (OS_MONTHS_DMT, sample-level OVERALL_SURVIVAL_MONTHS, OS_MONTHS_DIAG_TO_COLL) can start at different points. Pair time and status only within the same definition and never mix them across pairs.

findings.question: When survival is measured from diagnosis but genomic profiling happens later, what is the recommended way to correct for left truncation (immortal time) in Cox models, and how large is the bias typically?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB (gateway HTTP 403). Background knowledge only: use delayed entry (left-truncation risk-set adjustment). This is a counting-process Cox model, Surv(entry = diagnosis-to-sequencing time, exit = OS from diagnosis, event), or entry_col in lifelines. The alternative is to measure OS from the sequencing date. Without the correction, real-world genomic cohorts tend to overstate survival, often by months, and hazard ratios become biased for genotypes that tend to be sequenced late. A loss of significance under delayed entry, as Team A found, suggests the uncorrected STK11 effect is partly an artifact, so prefer the corrected estimate. I could not verify the size of the bias from a source.

findings.question: In survival analyses of a gene altered in about 10 of 100 patients, what minimum events per variable and which methods (e.g. Firth penalised Cox) are recommended to judge whether that gene is an independent prognostic factor?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB (gateway HTTP 403). Background knowledge only: the usual rule is about 10 events per variable (Peduzzi 1995); Vittinghoff & McCulloch 2007 found 5-9 often acceptable. With a rare binary covariate, the number of events among carriers is the real limit. The recommended method is Firth-penalised Cox (Heinze & Schemper 2001; R package coxphf) with profile-likelihood confidence intervals and as few covariates as possible. Only about 10 altered patients cannot support a firm claim of independent association, and a non-significant result there means the analysis is underpowered, not that there is no effect.
